claim: HIV-1 Vpu exerts broad immunosuppressive effects by inhibiting activation of the transcription factor NF-κB.
source: Here, we show that the accessory viral protein U (Vpu) of HIV-1 exerts broad immunosuppressive effects by inhibiting activation of the transcription factor NF-κB.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches including RNA-Seq, gene set enrichment analyses, and cytokine arrays as described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Vpu-deficient HIV-1 strains induce substantially stronger immune responses than the respective wild type viruses.
source: Global transcriptional profiling of infected CD4 +T cells revealed that vpu-deficient HIV-1 strains induce substantially stronger immune responses than the respective wild type viruses.
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-Seq data comparing wild type and vpu-deficient viruses across multiple donors and viral strains.

claim: Vpu suppresses the expression of NF-κB targets including interferons and restriction factors.
source: Gene set enrichment analyses and cytokine arrays showed that Vpu suppresses the expression of NF-κB targets including interferons and restriction factors.
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analyses and cytokine array data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The immunosuppressive activity of Vpu is independent of its ability to counteract the restriction factor and innate sensor tetherin.
source: Mutational analyses demonstrated that this immunosuppressive activity of Vpu is independent of its ability to counteract the restriction factor and innate sensor tetherin.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the use of selective Vpu mutants that separate tetherin antagonism from NF-κB inhibition.

claim: Vpu-mediated inhibition of immune activation required an arginine residue in the cytoplasmic domain that is critical for blocking NF-κB signaling downstream of tetherin.
source: However, Vpu-mediated inhibition of immune activation required an arginine residue in the cytoplasmic domain that is critical for blocking NF-κB signaling downstream of tetherin.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutational analysis of specific arginine residues (R45K in subtype B, R50K in subtype C).

claim: HIV-1 Vpu potently suppresses NF-κB-elicited antiviral immune responses at the transcriptional level.
source: In summary, our findings demonstrate that HIV-1 Vpu potently suppresses NF-κB-elicited antiviral immune responses at the transcriptional level.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by the entire body of experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: HIV replicates and spreads successfully in its human host, still infecting about 2 million individuals each year.
source: Nevertheless, HIV replicates and spreads successfully in its human host, still infecting about 2 million individuals each year.
evidence: This is a statement about HIV epidemiology based on established knowledge.

claim: The success of HIV-1 in part depends on four so-called accessory proteins (Vif, Nef, Vpr, and Vpu).
source: The success of HIV-1 in part depends on four so-called accessory proteins (Vif, Nef, Vpr, and Vpu).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations to previous work.

claim: HIV-1 accessory proteins are dispensable for viral replication in vitro, but are essential for high viral loads and efficient spread in vivo.
source: These viral proteins can be dispensable for viral replication in vitro, but are essential for high viral loads and efficient spread in vivo since they antagonize a variety of innate immune sensors and/or effectors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The host restriction factors APOBEC3G, tetherin, and SERINC5 are counteracted by Vif, Vpu, and Nef, respectively.
source: The host restriction factors APOBEC3G, tetherin, and SERINC5, for example are counteracted by Vif, Vpu, and Nef, respectively (Chemudupati et al., 2019; Sauter and Kirchhoff, 2018; Simon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Lentiviral accessory proteins not only target specific components of the cellular immune response at the protein level, but exert broad inhibitory effects by suppressing antiviral immune responses also at the transcriptional level.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that lentiviral accessory proteins not only target specific components of the cellular immune response at the protein level, but exert broad inhibitory effects by suppressing antiviral immune responses also at the transcriptional level (Faust et al., 2017; Sauter and Kirchhoff, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Vif, Vpr, and Vpu have all been suggested to inhibit expression of interferon-β (IFN-β) and potentially other antiviral genes by depleting the cellular transcription factor IRF-3.
source: For example, Vif, Vpr, and Vpu have all been suggested to inhibit expression of interferon-β (IFN-β) and potentially other antiviral genes by depleting the cellular transcription factor IRF-3 (Doehle et al., 2012; Okumura et al., 2008; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Vpu-mediated degradation of IRF-3 has been challenged and the immunosuppressive activity of Vpu has been ascribed to its ability to inhibit NF-κB activation instead.
source: Vpu-mediated degradation of IRF-3, however, has been challenged and the immunosuppressive activity of Vpu has been ascribed to its ability to inhibit NF-κB activation instead (Hotter et al., 2013; Manganaro et al., 2015; Sauter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NF-κB is expressed in almost all cell types and governs the expression of hundreds of genes in response to infection.
source: NF-κB is expressed in almost all cell types and governs the expression of hundreds of genes in response to infection.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NF-κB.

claim: Well-described targets of NF-κB comprise pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, CXCL10, or IFN-β, as well as antiviral restriction factors including IFIT1 or ISG15.
source: Well-described targets of NF-κB comprise pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, CXCL10, or IFN-β, as well as antiviral restriction factors including IFIT1 or ISG15 (Hiscott et al., 1989; Libermann and Baltimore, 1990; Ohmori and Hamilton, 1993; Pfeffer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NF-κB-mediated immune activation fails to prevent HIV-1 infection.
source: Nevertheless, NF-κB-mediated immune activation fails to prevent HIV-1 infection.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HIV-1 pathogenesis.

claim: NF-κB activation and subsequent cytokine release may contribute to a detrimental chronic hyper-activation of the immune system that drives disease progression in HIV-infected individuals, even under effective antiretroviral therapy.
source: On the contrary, NF-κB activation and subsequent cytokine release may even contribute to a detrimental chronic hyper-activation of the immune system that drives disease progression in HIV-infected individuals, even under effective antiretroviral therapy (Miedema et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: NF-κB binding sites are present in the lentiviral long terminal repeat (LTR) promoter and are essential for efficient HIV transcription and replication.
source: Furthermore, NF-κB binding sites are also present in the lentiviral long terminal repeat (LTR) promoter and are essential for efficient HIV transcription and replication (Calman et al., 1988; Chan and Greene, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Vpu of pandemic HIV-1 group M viruses counteracts tetherin, which not only inhibits virion release, but also acts as an innate sensor activating canonical NF-κB signaling upon detection of viral infection.
source: First, Vpu of pandemic HIV-1 group M viruses counteracts tetherin, which not only inhibits virion release, but also acts as an innate sensor activating canonical NF-κB signaling upon detection of viral infection (Galão et al., 2012; Sauter et al., 2013; Tokarev et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Vpu stabilizes IκB, the inhibitor of NF-κB, and prevents the nuclear translocation of NF-κB independently of tetherin.
source: Second, Vpu stabilizes IκB, the inhibitor of NF-κB, and prevents the nuclear translocation of NF-κB independently of tetherin (Akari et al., 2001; Bour et al., 2001; Leulier et al., 2003; Sauter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The effects of Vpu and the relative contribution of both mechanisms on global cellular gene expression and immune activation remained unclear.
source: However, despite the key role of NF-κB in immune activation, the effects of Vpu and the relative contribution of both mechanisms on global cellular gene expression and immune activation remained unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: RNA-Seq analyses of human CD4 +T cells infected with primary HIV-1 clones containing intact, disrupted, or selectively mutated vpu genes were performed.
source: Here, we performed RNA-Seq analyses of human CD4 +T cells infected with primary HIV-1 clones containing intact, disrupted, or selectively mutated vpu genes.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Transcription factor network analyses revealed that Vpu preferentially suppresses the expression of NF-κB target genes involved in adaptive and innate immune responses.
source: Transcription factor network analyses revealed that Vpu preferentially suppresses the expression of NF-κB target genes involved in adaptive and innate immune responses, such as antigen processing, major histocompatibility complex I (MHC-I) presentation, type I IFN signaling or DNA/RNA sensing.
evidence: This is based on transcription factor network analyses of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Vpu suppressed expression of cellular host restriction factors (e.g. IFIT1-3, ISG15).
source: Furthermore, Vpu suppressed expression of cellular host restriction factors (e.g. IFIT1-3, ISG15) and reduced the expression and release of IFNs and other pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. IL-6, CXCL10) from HIV-1 infected cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data and cytokine measurements.

claim: Vpu reduced the expression and release of IFNs and other pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. IL-6, CXCL10) from HIV-1 infected cells.
source: Furthermore, Vpu suppressed expression of cellular host restriction factors (e.g. IFIT1-3, ISG15) and reduced the expression and release of IFNs and other pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. IL-6, CXCL10) from HIV-1 infected cells.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and cytokine array data.

claim: There is no evidence for Vpu-mediated inhibition of IRF3-driven gene expression.
source: In contrast to previous findings, we found no evidence for Vpu-mediated inhibition of IRF3-driven gene expression.
evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data analysis which did not show enrichment of IRF3 target genes among Vpu-suppressed genes.

claim: Inhibition of NF-κB and the immunosuppressive effects of Vpu depend on an arginine residue in its first cytoplasmic alpha-helix.
source: Mutational analyses revealed that inhibition of NF-κB and the immunosuppressive effects of Vpu depend on an arginine residue in its first cytoplasmic alpha-helix, while its ability to counteract the host restriction factor and innate sensor tetherin is dispensable.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutational analysis and functional assays.

claim: The ability of Vpu to counteract the host restriction factor and innate sensor tetherin is dispensable for its immunosuppressive effects.
source: Mutational analyses revealed that inhibition of NF-κB and the immunosuppressive effects of Vpu depend on an arginine residue in its first cytoplasmic alpha-helix, while its ability to counteract the host restriction factor and innate sensor tetherin is dispensable.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the use of selective Vpu mutants.

claim: Three primary viral isolates CH293, CH077, and STCO1 were selected because they are derived from the most prevalent HIV-1 subtypes B and C and represent different stages of infection, different tropisms, and different risk factors.
source: We selected the three primary viral isolates CH293, CH077, and STCO1 since they are derived from the most prevalent HIV-1 subtypes B and C and represent different stages of infection (transmitted/founder or chronic viruses), different tropisms (R5/X4- or R5-tropic), and different risk factors (homo- or heterosexual) (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the rationale for selecting specific viral isolates for the study.

claim: A cytoplasmic arginine residue within Vpu was mutated to lysine (R45K in subtype B, R50K in subtype C) to abrogate IκB stabilization and NF-κB inhibition downstream of tetherin.
source: In order to abrogate IκB stabilization and NF-κB inhibition downstream of tetherin, a previously described cytoplasmic arginine residue within Vpu was mutated to lysine (R45K in subtype B, R50K in subtype C) (Pickering et al., 2014; Sauter et al., 2015; Yamada et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the mutagenesis strategy and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HIV-1 constructs lacking Vpu or expressing the R/K mutant Vpu induced significantly higher levels of NF-κB activation than the respective wild type viruses.
source: As expected, a luciferase-based reporter assay showed that HIV-1 constructs lacking Vpu or expressing the R/K mutant Vpu induced significantly higher levels of NF-κB activation than the respective wild type (wt) viruses (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The effects of Vpu on NF-κB activation were independent of tetherin since tetherin is not expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: These effects were independent of tetherin since tetherin is not expressed in HEK293T cells used in this experimental setup.
evidence: This is based on knowledge about tetherin expression in HEK293T cells.

claim: Loss-of-function in the R/K mutants was complete for CH293 and STCO1, but only partial for CH077.
source: Comparison with fully Vpu-deficient mutants (vpu stop) revealed that loss-of-function in the R/K mutants was complete for CH293 and STCO1, but only partial for CH077.
evidence: This is based on comparison of NF-κB activation levels between different mutants.

claim: Vpu-mediated suppression of NF-κB activity was associated with reduced nuclear translocation of p65.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy showed that Vpu-mediated suppression of NF-κB activity was associated with reduced nuclear translocation of p65 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy data.

claim: Mutations in an alanine interface in the transmembrane domain of Vpu (A15L/A19L in subtype B, A20L/A24L in subtype C) abrogated the ability of all three viruses to decrease tetherin surface levels.
source: In agreement with published data (Kmiec et al., 2016; Vigan and Neil, 2010), mutations in an alanine interface in the transmembrane domain of Vpu (A15L/A19L in subtype B, A20L/A24L in subtype C) abrogated the ability of all three viruses to decrease tetherin surface levels (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The AA/LL mutations abrogated the ability of Vpu to counteract tetherin-mediated restriction of virus release.
source: In agreement with published data (Kmiec et al., 2016; Vigan and Neil, 2010), mutations in an alanine interface in the transmembrane domain of Vpu (A15L/A19L in subtype B, A20L/A24L in subtype C) abrogated the ability of all three viruses to decrease tetherin surface levels (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) and to counteract tetherin-mediated restriction of virus release (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by virus release assay data.

claim: The AA/LL mutations had no effect on tetherin-independent NF-κB activation.
source: However, the AA/LL mutations had no effect on tetherin-independent NF-κB activation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the NF-κB reporter assay data.

claim: The R/K mutations had no significant effect on Vpu-mediated tetherin counteraction.
source: Vice versa, the R/K mutations had no significant effect on Vpu-mediated tetherin counteraction (Figure 1D and E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and virus release assay data.

claim: The AA/LL and R/K mutants were expressed as efficiently as wild type Vpu.
source: In agreement with their selective phenotype, the AA/LL and R/K mutants were expressed as efficiently as wild type Vpu (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data.

claim: RNA sequencing was performed three days post-infection to enable rapid and deep profiling of transcripts.
source: Three days post-infection, RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) was performed to enable rapid and deep profiling of transcripts.
evidence: This describes the experimental timeline and approach.

claim: The sequencing of infected cells from four healthy donors yielded 24.6 to 51.9 million reads per sample and an average sequence coverage of 82.6%.
source: The sequencing of infected cells from four healthy donors (two women, two men) (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1) yielded 24.6 to 51.9 million reads per sample and an average sequence coverage of 82.6% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the RNA-Seq data quality metrics.

claim: No sample outliers were detected based on principal component analysis and considering Cook's distance.
source: No sample outliers were detected based on principal component analysis and considering Cook's distance, which measures the influence on fitted coefficients for a gene by a single sample (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the quality control analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Samples are clustered by donor and virus rather than the vpu genotype.
source: Principal component analyses revealed four major clusters, with the donor background accounting for the highest variation in gene expression (Figure 2B). Within each donor, the identity of the viral isolate (i.e. CH293, CH077, and STCO1) had more pronounced effects on the cellular transcriptome than the vpu genotype (i.e. wt, vpu stop, R/K, AA/LL).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: The donor background accounted for the highest variation in gene expression.
source: Principal component analyses revealed four major clusters, with the donor background accounting for the highest variation in gene expression (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Within each donor, the identity of the viral isolate had more pronounced effects on the cellular transcriptome than the vpu genotype.
source: Within each donor, the identity of the viral isolate (i.e. CH293, CH077, and STCO1) had more pronounced effects on the cellular transcriptome than the vpu genotype (i.e. wt, vpu stop, R/K, AA/LL).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Higher infection rates resulted in a higher number of differentially expressed genes.
source: In agreement with the latter hypothesis, higher infection rates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) resulted in a higher number of differentially expressed genes.
evidence: This is based on correlation between infection rates and number of differentially expressed genes.

claim: HIV-1 CH077 (infecting 60–80% of all CD4 +T cells) significantly modulated the expression of 4202 genes.
source: For example, HIV-1 CH077 (infecting 60–80% of all CD4 +T cells) significantly modulated the expression of 4202 genes, while CH293 (infecting 20–40% of the cells) resulted in only 1565 differentially expressed genes and STCO1 (infecting 30–60% of the cells) had an intermediate phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: CH293 (infecting 20–40% of the cells) resulted in only 1565 differentially expressed genes.
source: For example, HIV-1 CH077 (infecting 60–80% of all CD4 +T cells) significantly modulated the expression of 4202 genes, while CH293 (infecting 20–40% of the cells) resulted in only 1565 differentially expressed genes and STCO1 (infecting 30–60% of the cells) had an intermediate phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: STCO1 (infecting 30–60% of the cells) had an intermediate phenotype.
source: For example, HIV-1 CH077 (infecting 60–80% of all CD4 +T cells) significantly modulated the expression of 4202 genes, while CH293 (infecting 20–40% of the cells) resulted in only 1565 differentially expressed genes and STCO1 (infecting 30–60% of the cells) had an intermediate phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Infectious viral doses of the mutants were adjusted to the respective wt viruses for unbiased analysis of the effect of specific Vpu functions on host gene expression.
source: Importantly, infectious viral doses of the mutants were adjusted to the respective wt viruses for unbiased analysis of the effect of specific Vpu functions on host gene expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This describes an important experimental control.

claim: Combined analysis of all three viral isolates revealed that 3369 genes were differentially expressed comparing wt to mock infected CD4 +T cells (1587 up- and 1782 down-regulated).
source: Combined analysis of all three viral isolates revealed that 3369 genes were differentially expressed comparing wt to mock infected CD4 +T cells (1587 up- and 1782 down-regulated) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: HIV-1 suppresses pathways involved in transcription, translation, cell division and energy metabolism.
source: Gene set enrichment analyses (KEGG) demonstrated that HIV-1 suppresses pathways involved in transcription, translation, cell division and energy metabolism (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: 'Spliceosome', 'RNA transport' and 'ribosome biogenesis' were among the most strongly inhibited pathways.
source: In agreement with previous analyses in infected T cell lines (Chang et al., 2011; Kleinman et al., 2014), 'spliceosome', 'RNA transport' and 'ribosome biogenesis' were among the most strongly inhibited pathways.
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway analysis and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Gene sets involved in (antiviral) immunity including 'chemokine signaling', 'T cell receptor signaling' and 'antigen processing and presentation' were induced upon wt HIV-1 infection.
source: In contrast, gene sets involved in (antiviral) immunity including 'chemokine signaling', 'T cell receptor signaling' and 'antigen processing and presentation' were induced upon wt HIV-1 infection (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Upon complete loss of Vpu (vpu stop vs. wt), 92 genes were differentially expressed (54 up, 38 down) across the three HIV-1 clones and four donors tested.
source: To determine the contribution of Vpu to the effects of HIV-1 on host gene expression, we compared the transcriptomes of mutant vs. wt infected cells. Upon complete loss of Vpu (vpu stop vs. wt), 92 genes were differentially expressed (54 up, 38 down) across the three HIV-1 clones and four donors tested, while seven genes (six up, one down) were differentially expressed upon selective loss of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition (NF-κB-def. Vpu mutant vs. wt) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Seven genes (six up, one down) were differentially expressed upon selective loss of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition (NF-κB-def. Vpu mutant vs. wt).
source: To determine the contribution of Vpu to the effects of HIV-1 on host gene expression, we compared the transcriptomes of mutant vs. wt infected cells. Upon complete loss of Vpu (vpu stop vs. wt), 92 genes were differentially expressed (54 up, 38 down) across the three HIV-1 clones and four donors tested, while seven genes (six up, one down) were differentially expressed upon selective loss of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition (NF-κB-def. Vpu mutant vs. wt) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: All six genes that were upregulated upon introduction of the R/K mutation (i.e. GNG4, NFKBIA, RGS1, NFE2L3, SDC4, NFKB2) were also induced upon complete loss of Vpu.
source: Notably, all six genes that were upregulated upon introduction of the R/K mutation (i.e. GNG4, NFKBIA, RGS1, NFE2L3, SDC4, NFKB2) were also induced upon complete loss of Vpu.
evidence: This is based on comparison of differentially expressed genes between different mutants.

claim: Abrogation of tetherin counteraction did not significantly affect the expression of any of the genes analyzed (tetherin-def. Vpu mutant vs. wt).
source: In comparison, abrogation of tetherin counteraction did not significantly affect the expression of any of the genes analyzed (tetherin-def. Vpu mutant vs. wt) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: The AA/LL mutant is still able to prevent NF-κB activation downstream of tetherin.
source: This agrees with our result that the AA/LL mutants is still able to prevent NF-κB activation downstream of tetherin (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on the NF-κB reporter assay data.

claim: Vpu preferentially suppresses the expression of NF-κB target genes, with gene sets regulated by other transcription factors (including IRFs) playing only a minor role.
source: This unbiased approach revealed that Vpu preferentially suppresses the expression of NF-κB target genes, with gene sets regulated by other transcription factors (including IRFs) playing only a minor role (Figure 3B, left panel).
evidence: This is based on transcription factor network analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Genes upregulated by Vpu showed no enrichment of NF-κB target genes.
source: In contrast, genes upregulated by Vpu (Figure 3B, right panel) showed no enrichment of NF-κB target genes.
evidence: This is based on transcription factor network analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: About 3% of cellular transcripts covered by the RNA-Seq approach are NF-κB inducible.
source: Of the more than 26.000 cellular transcripts covered by our RNA-Seq approach, about 3% are NF-κB inducible (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of NF-κB target genes in the dataset.

claim: The percentage of NF-κB inducible genes increases to 30% in genes whose expression is up-regulated upon complete loss of Vpu.
source: This percentage increases to 30% and 67% in genes, whose expression is up-regulated upon complete loss of Vpu or selective loss of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of NF-κB target genes among differentially expressed genes.

claim: The percentage of NF-κB inducible genes increases to 67% in genes whose expression is up-regulated upon selective loss of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition.
source: This percentage increases to 30% and 67% in genes, whose expression is up-regulated upon complete loss of Vpu or selective loss of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of NF-κB target genes among differentially expressed genes.

claim: None of 34 previously identified IRF3 targets were found among the transcripts decreased in the presence of Vpu.
source: In contrast, we did not find any of 34 previously identified IRF3 targets (Grandvaux et al., 2002) among the transcripts decreased in the presence of Vpu (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on analysis of IRF3 target genes in the dataset.

claim: IFN-stimulated genes were enriched among genes suppressed by Vpu.
source: In agreement with a key role of NF-κB in antiviral immunity, IFN-stimulated genes were also enriched among genes suppressed by Vpu (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ISGs among differentially expressed genes.

claim: Vpu preferentially inhibits the induction of pathways involved in innate and adaptive immunity including 'response to type I IFN' and 'antigen processing and MHC I presentation'.
source: GO and KEGG gene set enrichment analyses demonstrated that Vpu preferentially inhibits the induction of pathways involved in innate and adaptive immunity including 'response to type I IFN' and 'antigen processing and MHC I presentation' (Figure 3D, left panel).
evidence: This is based on GO and KEGG pathway analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: 'Cytosolic DNA sensing' and 'RIG-I like receptors' were not significantly induced by wt HIV-1 infection, but markedly upregulated upon disruption of vpu.
source: Intriguingly, 'cytosolic DNA sensing' and 'RIG-I like receptors' were not significantly induced by wt HIV-1 infection, but markedly upregulated upon disruption of vpu (Figures 2D and 3D left panel).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: A similar phenotype was observed upon selective abrogation of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition, strongly suggesting that these immunosuppressive effects of Vpu depend on its ability to prevent NF-κB activation.
source: A similar phenotype was observed upon selective abrogation of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition (Figure 3D, right panel), strongly suggesting that these immunosuppressive effects of Vpu depend on its ability to prevent NF-κB activation.
evidence: This is based on comparison of pathway analysis results between different mutants.

claim: Several host restriction factors (e.g. IFIT1, ISG15, HERC5) are expressed in an NF-κB-dependent manner.
source: As several host restriction factors (e.g. IFIT1, ISG15, HERC5) are expressed in an NF-κB-dependent manner (Kroismayr et al., 2004; Pfeffer et al., 2004), we defined two additional custom gene sets: 'NF-κB target genes' (Supplementary file 2; http://bioinfo.lifl.fr/NF-KB/) and 'Host restriction factors' (Supplementary file 3; Kluge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both 'NF-κB target genes' and 'Host restriction factors' gene sets were significantly upregulated upon loss of Vpu or Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition.
source: Again, both of them were significantly upregulated upon loss of Vpu or Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition (Figure 3D, bottom).
evidence: This is based on custom gene set enrichment analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Vpu significantly reduced mRNA levels of the host restriction factors APOBEC3B, HERC5, IFIT1-3, IFITM3, ISG15, MxA, OAS1 and Viperin, as well as IFN-β.
source: Analysis of individual genes revealed that Vpu significantly reduced mRNA levels of the host restriction factors APOBEC3B, HERC5, IFIT1-3, IFITM3, ISG15, MxA, OAS1 and Viperin, as well as IFN-β (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of individual gene expression levels from the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Lack of Vpu-dependent inhibition of NF-κB activation was associated with 2- to 11-fold increased IFN-β mRNA expression levels in HIV-1 infected CD4 +T cells.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR confirmed that lack of Vpu-dependent inhibition of NF-κB activation was associated with 2- to 11-fold increased IFN-β mRNA expression levels in HIV-1 infected CD4 +T cells (Figure 4A, top panels).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR validation of the RNA-Seq results.

claim: In case of HIV-1 CH077, the R45K mutation had only modest effects, which is in agreement with its incomplete loss of NF-κB inhibition.
source: In case of HIV-1 CH077, the R45K mutation had only modest effects, which is in agreement with its incomplete loss of NF-κB inhibition (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of qRT-PCR results with NF-κB reporter assay data.

claim: The effects of the viruses on IFN-β induction correlated well with their modulation of NF-κB activity.
source: Overall, the effects of the viruses on IFN-β induction correlated well with their modulation of NF-κB activity (Figure 4A, bottom panels).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between IFN-β expression and NF-κB activity.

claim: Differences in IFN-β expression were not a consequence of different infection rates.
source: Importantly, differences in IFN-β expression were not a consequence of different infection rates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on comparison of IFN-β expression with infection rates.

claim: The AA/LL mutations abrogating tetherin counteraction had no marked effect on CXCL10 or IL-6 production.
source: The AA/LL mutations abrogating tetherin counteraction had no marked effect on CXCL10 or IL-6 production.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry-based cytokine quantification.

claim: Loss of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition increased expression of CXCL10 and IL-6 by 50% to 300%.
source: In contrast, loss of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition increased expression of these pro-inflammatory cytokines by 50% to 300% (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry-based cytokine quantification.

claim: Vpu suppressed the production of MIP-1β/CCL4, RANTES/CCL5, TNF-α/-β, IFN-γ and many additional cytokines in an NF-κB-dependent manner.
source: In addition to CXCL10 and IL-6, Vpu suppressed the production of MIP-1β/CCL4, RANTES/CCL5, TNF-α/-β, IFN-γ and many additional cytokines in an NF-κB-dependent manner (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on membrane array-based cytokine detection.

claim: Complete lack of Vpu resulted in 32% increases of NF-κB-inducible cytokine levels on average.
source: On average, complete lack of Vpu resulted in 32% and the single R45K mutation in 24% increases of NF-κB-inducible cytokine levels, respectively.
evidence: This is based on analysis of cytokine array data.

claim: The single R45K mutation resulted in 24% increases of NF-κB-inducible cytokine levels on average.
source: On average, complete lack of Vpu resulted in 32% and the single R45K mutation in 24% increases of NF-κB-inducible cytokine levels, respectively.
evidence: This is based on analysis of cytokine array data.

claim: Immune-modulatory functions are frequently impaired in lab-adapted HIV-1 strains.
source: Since immune-modulatory functions are frequently impaired in lab-adapted HIV-1 strains (Apps et al., 2016; Pickering et al., 2014), we exclusively used clones representing primary HIV-1 isolates, including one transmitted/founder virus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Transmitted/founder viruses establish successful infection upon transmission and are characterized by an increased resistance to type I IFNs.
source: The latter establish successful infection upon transmission and are characterized by an increased resistance to type I IFNs that enables efficient replication in an environment of augmented immune activation observed during acute infection (Iyer et al., 2017; Parrish et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Selective abrogation of tetherin antagonism did not significantly change host gene expression.
source: Selective abrogation of tetherin antagonism did not significantly change host gene expression, demonstrating that tetherin-independent inhibition of NF-κB activation is sufficient for the immunosuppressive activity of Vpu.
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis of the tetherin-deficient mutant.

claim: Tetherin-independent inhibition of NF-κB activation is sufficient for the immunosuppressive activity of Vpu.
source: Selective abrogation of tetherin antagonism did not significantly change host gene expression, demonstrating that tetherin-independent inhibition of NF-κB activation is sufficient for the immunosuppressive activity of Vpu.
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis comparing different Vpu mutants.

claim: Introduction of the R/K mutation had much less pronounced effects on host gene expression than complete disruption of Vpu.
source: Nevertheless, introduction of the R/K mutation had much less pronounced effects on host gene expression than complete disruption of Vpu (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C,D).
evidence: This is based on comparison of differentially expressed genes between different mutants.

claim: Differences between R/K mutant and complete Vpu disruption may be explained by NF-κB-independent effects of Vpu on transcription and/or result from an only partial loss of NF-κB inhibition in the R/K mutants.
source: These differences may be explained by NF-κB-independent effects of Vpu on transcription and/or result from an only partial loss of NF-κB inhibition in the R/K mutants (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The exact pathways triggering NF-κB activation in HIV-1 infected CD4 +T cells remain to be determined.
source: The exact pathways triggering NF-κB activation in HIV-1 infected CD4 +T cells remain to be determined.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: A number of innate HIV sensors (e.g. IFI16, cGAS, PQBP1) have been shown to efficiently induce the activation of IRF3 and/or IRF7.
source: Although a number of innate HIV sensors (e.g. IFI16, cGAS, PQBP1) have been shown to efficiently induce the activation of IRF3 and/or IRF7 (Jakobsen et al., 2013; Krapp et al., 2018; Yoh et al., 2015), their relative contribution to NF-κB activation is still unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The relative contribution of innate HIV sensors to NF-κB activation is still unclear.
source: Although a number of innate HIV sensors (e.g. IFI16, cGAS, PQBP1) have been shown to efficiently induce the activation of IRF3 and/or IRF7 (Jakobsen et al., 2013; Krapp et al., 2018; Yoh et al., 2015), their relative contribution to NF-κB activation is still unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Activation via the T cell receptor complex may be an important determinant of NF-κB activation.
source: Besides pattern recognition receptors, activation via the T cell receptor complex may be an important determinant of NF-κB activation (Jamieson et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The unbiased approach does not confirm previous studies suggesting that Vpu suppresses the expression of IRF-3 target genes.
source: While our unbiased approach supports the hypothesis that Vpu preferentially targets NF-κB-driven gene expression, it does not confirm previous studies suggesting that Vpu suppresses the expression of IRF-3 target genes (Doehle et al., 2012; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data analysis which did not show enrichment of IRF3 target genes.

claim: Some of the genes targeted by Vpu share a regulation by IRF-1, IRF-2 and/or IRF-8/ICSBP.
source: Interestingly, however, some of the genes targeted by Vpu share a regulation by IRF-1, IRF-2 and/or IRF-8/ICSBP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on transcription factor network analysis.

claim: IRF-1, IRF-2 and IRF-8 are IFN-γ-inducible and may cooperate with each other to prevent prolonged expression of IFN-stimulated genes.
source: These transcription factors are IFN-γ-inducible and may cooperate with each other to prevent prolonged expression of IFN-stimulated genes (Elser et al., 2002; Horiuchi et al., 2011; Kuwata et al., 2002; Tamura et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The observed effect of Vpu on IRF-1, -2 and -8 and their target genes may only be indirect since Vpu reduced the release of IFN-γ, an NF-κB target gene, from infected cells.
source: However, the observed effect of Vpu on IRF-1,–2 and −8 and their target genes may only be indirect since Vpu reduced the release of IFN-γ, an NF-κB target gene, from infected cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cytokine data.

claim: All the cytokines suppressed by Vpu (IFN-β, CXCL10/IP-10, IL-6 and TNF-α) are part of the cytokine storm during acute lentiviral infection.
source: Besides IFN-γ, Vpu also suppressed the production of other cytokines, including IFN-β, CXCL10/IP-10, IL-6 and TNF-α (Figure 4), even in the context of PHA-prestimulated CD4 +T cells. All these factors are part of the cytokine storm during acute lentiviral infection (Abel et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2016; Stacey et al., 2009), but fail to eliminate the virus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines may contribute to disease progression and accelerate pathogenesis of AIDS by inducing prolonged hyper-activation of the immune system.
source: These pro-inflammatory cytokines may even contribute to disease progression and accelerate pathogenesis of AIDS by inducing prolonged hyper-activation of the immune system.
evidence: This is a speculation based on established knowledge.

claim: Increased plasma levels of CXCL10, TNF-α and IL-6 are associated with accelerated loss of CD4 +T cells in HIV-1 infected individuals.
source: For example, increased plasma levels of CXCL10, TNF-α and IL-6 are associated with accelerated loss of CD4 +T cells in HIV-1 infected individuals (Borges et al., 2015; Liovat et al., 2012; Vaidya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During primary HIV-1 infection, CXCL10 plasma levels predict disease progression even better than plasma viral loads or CD4 +T cell counts.
source: During primary HIV-1 infection, CXCL10 plasma levels predict disease progression even better than plasma viral loads or CD4 +T cell counts (Liovat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: By modulating cellular cytokine production, Vpu may be an important determinant of HIV-1 pathogenesis.
source: By modulating cellular cytokine production, Vpu may therefore be an important determinant of HIV-1 pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and established knowledge.

claim: The suppression of immune activation by Vpu is incomplete, and wt HIV-1 still triggers the activation of a variety of immune signaling pathways.
source: Notably, however, the suppression of immune activation by Vpu is incomplete, and wt HIV-1 still triggers the activation of a variety of immune signaling pathways, including T cell, B cell, Fc and Toll-like receptor signaling (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: 'RIG-I-like receptors' and 'cytosolic DNA sensing' were the only immunity-related KEGG pathways that were not significantly upregulated upon wt HIV-1 infection.
source: In fact, 'RIG-I-like receptors' and 'cytosolic DNA sensing' were the only immunity-related KEGG pathways that were not significantly upregulated upon wt HIV-1 infection (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Incomplete suppression of NF-κB activation and/or the induction of pathways involving transcription factors that are not directly targeted by Vpu may underlie the detrimental immune activation that drives disease progression in HIV-1 infected individuals.
source: Thus, incomplete suppression of NF-κB activation and/or the induction of pathways involving transcription factors that are not directly targeted by Vpu may underlie the detrimental immune activation that drives disease progression in HIV-1 infected individuals.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data.

claim: The promoters of many restriction factors contain both NF-κB- and IRF-responsive elements.
source: The promoters of many restriction factors contain both NF-κB- and IRF-responsive elements (Pfeffer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The increase in restriction factor expression may be a direct consequence of missing Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition and/or the result of elevated cytokine levels.
source: Thus, this increase may either be a direct consequence of missing Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition and/or the result of elevated cytokine levels.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: HIV-1 uses Vpu to evade certain restriction factors by counteracting them at the transcriptional level.
source: Our data suggest that HIV-1 uses Vpu to evade certain restriction factors by counteracting them at the transcriptional level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing reduced restriction factor expression.

claim: Vpu has been previously shown to not only target tetherin at the protein level, but also reduce its mRNA expression.
source: In agreement with this, we have previously shown that Vpu not only targets tetherin at the protein level, but also reduces its mRNA expression (Sauter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Although many restriction factors are constitutively expressed, their expression and hence antiviral effect usually increases upon infection and/or IFN simulation.
source: Although many restriction factors are constitutively expressed, their expression and hence antiviral effect usually increases upon infection and/or IFN simulation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about restriction factors.

claim: Vpu-mediated suppression of transcription may considerably relieve restriction.
source: Thus, Vpu-mediated suppression of transcription may considerably relieve restriction.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and established knowledge.

claim: No direct HIV-1 antagonist has been identified for most restriction factors suppressed by Vpu (e.g. IFITs, HERC5, ISG15).
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note, that no direct HIV-1 antagonist has been identified for most restriction factors suppressed by Vpu (e.g. IFITs, HERC5, ISG15).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Vpu decreases cell surface levels of the NK cell activating ligands ULBP2/5/6.
source: For example, flow cytometric analyses of HIV-1 wt- and Δvpu-infected cells demonstrated that Vpu decreases cell surface levels of the NK cell activating ligands ULBP2/5/6 (Galaski et al., 2016) and the chemokine receptor CCR7 (Ramirez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Vpu decreases cell surface levels of the chemokine receptor CCR7.
source: For example, flow cytometric analyses of HIV-1 wt- and Δvpu-infected cells demonstrated that Vpu decreases cell surface levels of the NK cell activating ligands ULBP2/5/6 (Galaski et al., 2016) and the chemokine receptor CCR7 (Ramirez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RNA sequencing results suggest that Vpu does not (or at least not exclusively) target ULBP2 and CCR7 at the protein level but also prevents their expression by inhibiting the activation of NF-κB.
source: Our RNA sequencing results suggest that Vpu does not (or at least not exclusively) target these factors at the protein level but also prevents their expression by inhibiting the activation of NF-κB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-Seq data.

claim: The results are in agreement with the model that HIV-1 Nef boosts NF-κB activation during early stages of infection to initiate efficient transcription of viral genes, while Vpu suppresses NF-κB activation during later stages to limit antiviral gene expression of the host.
source: Furthermore, they are in agreement with the model that HIV-1 Nef boosts NF-κB activation during early stages of infection to initiate efficient transcription of viral genes, while Vpu suppresses NF-κB activation during later stages to limit antiviral gene expression of the host (Sauter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The importance of Vpu activity for viral replication, immune activation and disease progression during different stages of infection remains to be determined in vivo.
source: However, the importance of this Vpu activity for viral replication, immune activation and disease progression during different stages of infection remains to be determined in vivo.
evidence: This identifies a limitation and future direction.

claim: One limitation of the present study is the use of VSV-G for pseudotyping, which may influence sensing and overall gene expression.
source: One limitation of the present study is the use of VSV-G for pseudotyping, which may influence sensing and overall gene expression.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: The use of unsorted cells does not allow to discriminate between effects in infected and uninfected cells and may introduce a bias with respect to infection rates.
source: Furthermore, the use of unsorted cells does not allow to discriminate between effects in infected and uninfected cells and may introduce a bias with respect to infection rates.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: The potential confounder of using unsorted cells does not affect the comparison of wild type and vpu mutated viruses as the variants of each strain were normalized for their infectivity to obtain similar infection rates.
source: Nevertheless, this potential confounder does not affect the comparison of wild type and vpu mutated viruses as the variants of each strain were normalized for their infectivity to obtain similar infection rates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This addresses a potential concern about the experimental design.

claim: The present approach may underestimate the inhibitory effects of Vpu due to the presence of 25–80% uninfected bystander cells and the pre-activation of CD4 +T cells with PHA.
source: In fact, the present approach may even underestimate the inhibitory effects of Vpu due to the presence of 25–80% uninfected bystander cells and the pre-activation of CD4 +T cells with PHA.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential underestimation of effects.

claim: It remains to be clarified whether the inhibition of NF-κB activation by Vpu may compensate for the loss of Nef-mediated down-modulation of the T cell receptor CD3 in HIV-1 and its direct simian precursors.
source: It also remains to be clarified whether the inhibition of NF-κB activation by Vpu may compensate for the loss of Nef-mediated down-modulation of the T cell receptor CD3 in HIV-1 and its direct simian precursors.
evidence: This identifies a question for future research.

claim: The selective Vpu mutants generated in this study provide a valuable means to address questions about Vpu function in various in vivo models.
source: The selective Vpu mutants generated in this study provide a valuable means to address these questions in various in vivo models, including humanized mice (Yamada et al., 2015) and a recently established monkey model (Joas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the reagents generated in the study.

claim: An important role of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition for efficient viral spread and replication in vivo is supported by the observation that this activity is highly conserved among HIV-1 and closely related simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIV).
source: An important role of Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition for efficient viral spread and replication in vivo is supported by the observation that this activity is highly conserved among HIV-1 and closely related simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIV) (Sauter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: HIV-2 and the majority of SIV species, which do not encode Vpu, have evolved alternative mechanisms and prevent the activation of NF-κB via their accessory proteins Nef or Vpr.
source: In contrast, HIV-2 and the majority of SIV species, which do not encode Vpu, have evolved alternative mechanisms and prevent the activation of NF-κB via their accessory proteins Nef or Vpr (Hotter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Components of the canonical NF-κB signaling cascade are targeted by diverse virus families.
source: In fact, components of the canonical NF-κB signaling cascade are targeted by diverse virus families.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in virology.

claim: Polydnaviruses encode IκB-like proteins.
source: Well-described examples are IκB-like proteins encoded by polydnaviruses (Falabella et al., 2007), the Vaccinia virus K1 protein, which prevents the acetylation of RelA (Bravo Cruz and Shisler, 2016) or African swine fever virus A238L, which binds p65/NF-κB to prevent its nuclear translocation (Revilla et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Vaccinia virus K1 protein prevents the acetylation of RelA.
source: Well-described examples are IκB-like proteins encoded by polydnaviruses (Falabella et al., 2007), the Vaccinia virus K1 protein, which prevents the acetylation of RelA (Bravo Cruz and Shisler, 2016) or African swine fever virus A238L, which binds p65/NF-κB to prevent its nuclear translocation (Revilla et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: African swine fever virus A238L binds p65/NF-κB to prevent its nuclear translocation.
source: Well-described examples are IκB-like proteins encoded by polydnaviruses (Falabella et al., 2007), the Vaccinia virus K1 protein, which prevents the acetylation of RelA (Bravo Cruz and Shisler, 2016) or African swine fever virus A238L, which binds p65/NF-κB to prevent its nuclear translocation (Revilla et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Examples of convergent viral evolution highlight the importance of NF-κB in the antiviral immune response.
source: These examples of convergent viral evolution highlight the importance of NF-κB in the antiviral immune response and demonstrate that Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition is one of several sophisticated mechanisms that viruses have evolved to prevent the manifold immune responses triggered by this transcription factor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the examples of viral NF-κB antagonism.

claim: Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition is one of several sophisticated mechanisms that viruses have evolved to prevent the manifold immune responses triggered by this transcription factor.
source: These examples of convergent viral evolution highlight the importance of NF-κB in the antiviral immune response and demonstrate that Vpu-mediated NF-κB inhibition is one of several sophisticated mechanisms that viruses have evolved to prevent the manifold immune responses triggered by this transcription factor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and examples of viral NF-κB antagonism.
